scope: Visible whitelist only; semantic candidate supplement to measured nearest search

questions.stem: A Massachusetts collaborating pharmacist is issuing a prescription that another pharmacy will fill. Which particulars must she supply to the dispensing pharmacist? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Her home address, so that she can be reached outside working hours.
Her date of initial licensure in the Commonwealth.
Her registration number.
The name of her supervising physician.
Confirmation that the patient has consented to collaborative management.

questions.stem: An authorized pharmacist practising collaborative drug therapy management in a Massachusetts community pharmacy is asked during an inspection to produce the collaborative practice documents. Which statements about what this pharmacist is required to hold are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: The pharmacist must hold the signed original rather than a copy.
A copy of the current collaborative practice agreement must be maintained.
Copies of the current patient referral and patient consent must be included.
The documents must be maintained in the primary practice setting.
The documents must be readily retrievable when they are requested.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts collaborating pharmacist provides services on site at an assisted living residence that holds no health facility licence. She proposes to use a written medication order entered on the residence's own care record, as she does when working in a licensed hospice. What is the position?

choices.text: Permitted, because a written order is more rigorous than a prescription.
Permitted, because the residence maintains a care record for each resident.
Permitted, provided the supervising physician approves the residence in the agreement.
Not permitted, because the medication order route is unavailable outside a facility.
Not permitted, because a pharmacist may not provide services at a residence at all.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacist holds a current collaborative practice agreement that authorises her to administer vaccines. There is no Commissioner order in force for any designated vaccine, and the vaccine she is asked to give is not on the Department's eligible-medication administration list. May she give it?

choices.text: Yes, because the collaborative practice agreement authorises vaccine administration.
Yes, because vaccines fall outside the controlled substance framework entirely.
No, because a Commissioner order is needed before any vaccine may be given.
No, because the vaccine is absent from the eligible-medication list.
No, because a pharmacist may administer vaccines only in a hospital setting.

questions.stem: Two Massachusetts collaborating pharmacists each hold Department registration for the purpose of prescribing. One will prescribe only Schedule VI products under her agreement. The other will prescribe products in federally controlled schedules. Neither holds a DEA registration. What follows?

choices.text: Both are barred, because the regulation requires DEA registration of prescribers.
Neither is barred, because Department registration is the operative requirement.
The first may prescribe; the second needs DEA registration because it applies.
The second may prescribe; the first needs DEA registration for Schedule VI.
Both may prescribe, provided each notifies the DEA of the agreement's terms.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts collaborative practice agreement names three duties of the authorized pharmacist that may be delegated and two that may not. It says nothing further on the subject. The pharmacist proposes to delegate one of the named duties to trained staff for the next six weeks. What does the agreement still lack?

choices.text: Nothing further, once the delegable and non-delegable duties have been named.
Board approval of this particular delegation before it may take effect.
The when and how of delegation, together with its duration and its scope.
A separate written consent from the patient to the proposed delegation.
The supervising physician's countersignature on the delegation itself.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts collaborating pharmacist holds a Department registration for the purpose of prescribing and a valid agreement. She wishes to dispense a Schedule VI product for immediate treatment. That particular product is not among those her agreement authorises her to prescribe. May she do so?

choices.text: Yes, because immediate treatment is a separate power from prescribing.
Yes, because the product sits in Schedule VI, the least restricted schedule.
Yes, provided she notifies the supervising physician within 24 hours.
No, because the power runs only to substances she is authorised to prescribe.
No, because dispensing for immediate treatment requires a patient-specific order.

questions.stem: On the same morning a Massachusetts hospital pharmacist begins collaboratively managing an inpatient after a discussion about that patient with the attending supervising physician, and a community pharmacist begins collaboratively managing a walk-in after an identical discussion with her supervising physician. Neither holds a signed individual referral. Which analysis is correct?

choices.text: Both are properly referred, since a consultation is a referral in any setting.
The hospital pharmacist is properly referred; the community pharmacist is not.
The community pharmacist is properly referred; the hospital pharmacist is not.
Neither is properly referred, because a written referral is always required.
Neither is properly referred, because a referral must be signed to be effective.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts collaborating pharmacist resolves a Board matter by consent agreement that places a condition on her practice. She works under collaborative practice agreements with three supervising physicians. What does the regulation require her to do?

choices.text: Nothing further, because a consent agreement is not a Board order.
Notify only the physician whose agreement relates to the conduct at issue.
Notify the Board that the physicians have been informed, without contacting them.
Provide written notification of the discipline or practice restriction to each supervising physician.
Suspend all collaborative practice until the condition has been lifted.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts ambulatory care clinic has obtained approval from its medical staff executive committee for collaborative drug therapy management. The collaborating pharmacist works remotely from another site, reviewing records and speaking to patients by telephone. No physician is present with her. Is the arrangement compliant?

choices.text: Yes, because the correct approving body has approved the arrangement.
Yes, because the statute does not regulate where the pharmacist works.
Yes, provided the attending physician is reachable during clinic hours.
No, because the clinic setting requires on-site supervision by the attending physician.
No, because collaborative practice may not be conducted in an ambulatory care clinic.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist is evaluating the current statutory qualifications to enter a collaborative practice agreement. Which statements reflect M.G.L. c.112, § 24B1/2(b)? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Hold a current Massachusetts pharmacist license, currently practice in the Commonwealth, and maintain at least $1,000,000 of professional liability insurance.
Have earned a PharmD degree or completed five years of experience as a licensed pharmacist, or the equivalent.
Devote a portion of practice to the defined drug-therapy area and complete at least five additional related CE contact hours in each agreement year.
Apply for the statute's limited MassHealth ordering/referring participation if implementing regulations governing that participation are promulgated.
A pharmacist with a current PharmD must also complete five years of licensed-practice experience because the degree alternative is no longer recognized by statute.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts collaborating pharmacist wants an appropriately trained certified technician to collect the vital signs contemplated by her collaborative practice agreement. The agreement says nothing at all about delegation. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Silence in the agreement operates as permission to delegate the duty.
Delegation is permitted because the technician is appropriately trained.
Delegation is permitted because collecting vital signs is not a dispensing act.
The agreement must specify which of the pharmacist's duties may be delegated.
The agreement must specify which duties under it may not be delegated.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist is reviewing a proposed collaborative practice agreement before signing it. Which features does the statutory definition require for the agreement to be validly constituted? Select all that apply.

choices.text: It must be written and signed by the pharmacist and the supervising physician.
The collaborative practice may extend beyond the supervising physician's own scope.
It is subject to review and renewal on a biennial basis.
It must be filed with the Board before the pharmacist may act under it.
It must include individually developed guidelines for any prescriptive practice.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts collaborating pharmacist keeps the required documents on site. An investigator from the Board of Registration in Medicine asks to see them and the pharmacist answers that they are retrievable only to the Board of Registration in Pharmacy. Separately, the supervising physician has handed the pharmacist the original agreement for safekeeping. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: The pharmacist is right on retrievability and right to hold the original.
The pharmacist is right on retrievability but should return the original.
The pharmacist is wrong on retrievability and right to hold the original.
Both boards may request the documents, and the physician may pass the original on.
Both boards may request them, and the original belongs in the physician's record.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts supervising physician refers a patient for collaborative drug therapy management, records the referral and the patient's consent in his own chart, and tells the collaborating pharmacist that the documentation is complete and nothing further is needed. Where must the individual referral and consent be recorded?

choices.text: In the supervising physician's record alone, which is what the statute requires.
In the pharmacist's record alone, since the pharmacist delivers the service.
In whichever of the two records the professionals agree should hold them.
In the patient's record, by the pharmacist and by the supervising physician.
In a register filed with the Board, separately from the patient's record.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts health system is setting up collaborative drug therapy management across several of its sites. Which statements about who must approve it are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: In a licensed hospital, the Department of Public Health approves the arrangement.
A single system-wide approval suffices for every one of the listed settings.
In a long-term care facility, the facility's medical director or designee approves.
In a hospice setting, the hospice's medical director or designee approves.
An ambulatory care clinic additionally requires on-site physician supervision.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist is mapping out what a proposed collaborative practice agreement could cover. Which activities may fall within collaborative drug therapy management as the statute defines it? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Initiating, monitoring, modifying and discontinuing the patient's drug therapy.
Collecting and reviewing the patient's history.
Obtaining and checking pulse, temperature, blood pressure and respiration.
Settling a diagnosis where a laboratory result plainly supports one.
Ordering and evaluating laboratory tests directly related to the drug therapy.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts collaborating pharmacist rounding in a licensed long-term care facility decides to start a controlled substance for a resident. She writes what looks like an ordinary outpatient prescription and leaves it at the nurses' station. What does the regulation require instead?

choices.text: A prescription transmitted to the facility's contracted dispensing pharmacy.
A written medication order entered on the facility's own medical record for the resident.
A countersignature from the supervising physician on the prescription she wrote.
An oral order to the nurse on duty, confirmed in writing within 24 hours.
A referral back to the supervising physician, who must issue the order himself.

questions.stem: A retail collaborative practice agreement expressly allows initial Schedule VI prescriptions. The supervising physician referred an adult patient with hypertension, and the collaborating pharmacist issues an authorized Schedule VI antihypertensive prescription for that referred diagnosis late Friday afternoon. The physician's office will not reopen until Monday. What should the pharmacist do next?

choices.text: Arrange to send a copy of the prescription to the supervising physician within 24 hours rather than waiting for the office to reopen.
Wait until Monday because the 24-hour copy requirement excludes weekends and holidays.
Keep the prescription only in the pharmacy's collaborative-practice file unless the supervising physician later requests a copy.
Send the prescription copy to the Board within 24 hours and provide it to the supervising physician at the next scheduled review.
No copy is required because the agreement already authorizes initial Schedule VI prescribing for the referred diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old patient was referred to and consented to retail collaborative drug therapy management for hypertension under a written agreement that specifically covers hypertension. During a follow-up, the patient reports new recurrent wheezing and asks the pharmacist to diagnose asthma and start treatment. Asthma is not included in this patient's referral or current collaborative agreement. What is the most appropriate response?

choices.text: Manage the wheezing as asthma because asthma appears among disease states that may be eligible for retail collaborative management.
Diagnose asthma and begin treatment after obtaining a second patient consent, without changing the referral or agreement.
Begin asthma treatment now and have the supervising physician add asthma to the agreement retroactively by the end of the day.
Continue authorized hypertension management and return the new wheezing for physician evaluation before expanding collaborative management to that condition.
Manage the new condition without another referral because the individual-referral limitation applies only to controlled-substance therapy.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts collaborative practice agreement will lapse at the end of this month and will not be renewed. The pharmacist plans to write to each affected patient in the week after the lapse, explaining that the arrangement has ended and how their therapy will be continued. Which duty has already been missed?

choices.text: None; written notice after the lapse discharges both of the duties owed.
Notice to the Board of Registration in Pharmacy in advance of the lapse.
Notice to each affected patient's other prescribers in advance of the lapse.
A written variation of the agreement extending it beyond the lapse date.
Arranging an uninterrupted continuation of therapy before the lapse.

questions.stem: A referred patient at a Massachusetts retail pharmacy has run out of a medication her supervising physician prescribed, and the physician is unreachable. The collaborating pharmacist has never dispensed this patient a different medication for the same condition. What may the pharmacist do under the retail collaborative power?

choices.text: Initiate an equivalent medication for the same condition for up to 30 days.
Extend the current therapy the supervising physician prescribed by 30 days.
Extend the current therapy indefinitely until the physician can be reached.
Substitute a therapeutically similar agent and notify the physician afterwards.
Nothing, because the retail setting confers no continuation power at all.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts collaborative practice agreement was properly written, signed and within the supervising physician's scope when it was made twenty-six months ago. Neither party has reviewed it since. The pharmacist proposes to keep co-managing referred patients while a review is scheduled. What is the position?

choices.text: The agreement stands, because nothing in it has changed since it was signed.
The agreement stands, provided the pharmacist documents that a review is pending.
The agreement stands until the supervising physician gives notice of termination.
The agreement is out of currency, because review and renewal fall due biennially.
The agreement is void, and every act taken under it in month 25 must be reported.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist holds a current Department controlled substance registration that she obtained so that her pharmacy could dispense. She now has a valid collaborative practice agreement that includes prescriptive practices, and proposes to issue her first prescription. What does she still need?

choices.text: Nothing further; her current registration covers controlled substance activity.
A separate Board of Registration in Pharmacy licence category for prescribers.
The supervising physician's registration number recorded in the agreement.
A DEA registration, which is required for every collaborating pharmacist.
Department registration for the purpose of prescribing under 105 CMR 700.000.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist with no collaborative practice agreement, registered under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 7, wishes to keep a stock of a controlled substance for patient treatment and to administer it, relying on s. 9 alone. A physician in the same clinic, registered on the same basis, proposes to do the same. How do their positions differ?

choices.text: They do not differ; both are authorised by the same sentence of section 9.
They do not differ; both need a collaborative practice agreement to proceed.
The pharmacist may proceed and the physician needs a further instrument.
Neither may proceed, because section 9 confers no possession authority at all.
The physician may proceed; the pharmacist is limited by two further provisions.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist practising collaboratively in a retail drug business is reviewing what the statute permits her to do there. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Patients must be 18 years of age or older in that setting.
She may initiate a new Schedule II therapy whenever the referral identifies the diagnosis.
She may extend current therapy prescribed by the supervising physician by 30 days.
She may modify dosages of any medication the patient is currently taking.
She may administer vaccines under the terms of her agreement.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts collaborating pharmacist orders a laboratory test directly related to the drug therapy she co-manages, under an approved protocol for her setting and in direct consultation with the supervising physician, and then evaluates the result. Her evaluation concludes that the patient has a new condition. What is the position?

choices.text: The ordering may be proper, but the evaluation may not include a diagnostic component.
The ordering is improper, because a pharmacist may not order laboratory tests.
Both are proper, because the test was directly related to the therapy managed.
Both are improper, because laboratory work sits outside collaborative management.
Both are proper, provided she reports the conclusion to the supervising physician.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist takes a telephoned prescription from a collaborating pharmacist who gives her name, professional designation, registration number, work address and a callback number, but does not name the supervising physician. What should the receiving pharmacist do?

choices.text: Fill it, because the caller supplied the identifying particulars that matter.
Fill it, and record that the supervising physician was not identified.
Decline to fill it as transmitted until the supervising physician is named.
Decline to fill it, because a pharmacist may not telephone a prescription at all.
Fill it, provided she verifies the caller's registration number independently.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy proposes to engage a physician on two footings: to conduct quality assurance reviews of the pharmacists it employs who practise collaborative drug therapy management, and to enter into collaborative practice agreements with the pharmacy's patients. Which analysis is correct?

choices.text: Both engagements are permitted, since the pharmacy is not itself prescribing.
Both engagements are prohibited, since a retail pharmacy may not employ a physician.
The agreement engagement is permitted and the review engagement is prohibited.
Both are permitted if the physician's pay is unrelated to prescription volume.
The review engagement is permitted and the agreement engagement is prohibited.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts collaborating pharmacist plans to hold stock for dispensing for immediate treatment under her agreement. Which statements about how she may obtain it are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Any product she may prescribe may be bought from her usual wholesaler.
A Schedule IV product may be bought from a wholesaler for this purpose.
Schedule VI products she is authorised to prescribe may be ordered from a wholesaler.
Schedule II to V products may be bought from a distributor if properly recorded.
Schedule II to V products may come from the supervising physician or a patient's order.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacist is asked to begin collaboratively managing a walk-in who says her physician mentioned that the pharmacy could help with her blood pressure. Nothing is in writing and the pharmacist has had no contact with the physician. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: She is a collaborative patient because her own physician suggested it.
She is a collaborative patient because she has presented herself for the service.
The supervising physician must assess her and include a diagnosis on referral.
She becomes a collaborative patient once the pharmacist records the conversation.
In this setting she must be notified of and must consent to the services.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts collaborating pharmacist is negotiating an agreement that will include prescriptive practices. Which additional conditions attach because of that inclusion? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Holding at least $2,000,000 per occurrence of professional liability insurance.
Maintaining a current controlled substance registration issued by the Department during the term of the agreement.
Completing at least ten additional contact hours of continuing education each year of the agreement.
Submitting an attestation under the pains and penalties of perjury regarding MassHealth participation.
Obtaining a separate Board licence category for collaborating pharmacists.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts collaborating pharmacist completed her required collaborative practice continuing education two years ago and her current agreement was signed six months ago. She proposes to discard the older documentation. What does the regulation require?

choices.text: She may discard it, because the courses are now more than two years old.
She may discard it once her pharmacist registration has been renewed.
She must retain it for at least two years after the date of the current agreement.
She must retain it for the entire life of her pharmacist licence.
She must forward it to each supervising physician instead of retaining it.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts collaborative practice agreement authorises the pharmacist to modify the dosage of a named medication for a referred patient. Reviewing the patient, the pharmacist judges the medication should be stopped altogether. The agreement says nothing about stopping therapy. What may she do?

choices.text: She may not discontinue it, because that act must itself be authorised.
She may discontinue it, because stopping is a lesser step than modifying.
She may discontinue it, because it is a clinical rather than a prescribing act.
She may discontinue it once she notes the reason in the patient's record.
She may discontinue it only where the medication is in Schedule VI.

questions.stem: A community pharmacy receives an individually signed referral for a patient to enter a collaborative drug therapy management program. The document lists the patient's name and address, primary diagnosis, authorized comorbid diagnoses, and detailed treatment instructions. It does not state the patient's known allergies and contains no statement that the patient gave written informed consent. The pharmacist notes that the affiliated hospital often begins inpatient collaborative management through a consultation request that does not contain those two items. What is the best conclusion for the community-pharmacy referral?

choices.text: It is sufficient because a signed referral and specific treatment instructions replace the need for allergy and consent information.
It is sufficient if the hospital's consultation process would accept the same document.
It is incomplete because a community CDTM referral must include known allergies and a statement of written informed consent, in addition to the other required patient-specific information.
It is incomplete only if the patient has a known allergy that would change the treatment instructions.
It may be completed by treating the hospital's consultation request as an incorporated attachment, even though that request contains neither missing item.

questions.stem: A patient is receiving retail collaborative drug therapy management for diabetes. The supervising physician has also identified painful diabetic neuropathy as a co-morbidity and asks the collaborating pharmacist to initiate pregabalin (Schedule V), offering to countersign the pharmacist's order the same day. What is the best legal response?

choices.text: Initiate pregabalin because the physician identified the neuropathy as a co-morbidity of diabetes.
Initiate pregabalin if the supervising physician countersigns the pharmacist's order within 24 hours.
Do not initiate pregabalin under retail collaborative prescribing because the agreement cannot authorize prescribing Schedule II through V controlled substances.
Initiate a 30-day pregabalin supply because retail collaborative practice permits a 30-day extension of current therapy.
Initiate pregabalin because the retail prohibition applies to Schedule II through IV but not Schedule V.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts collaborating pharmacist holds two patient referrals. One is written in indelible pencil. The other arrived by email as a flattened image which the pharmacy system can neither store nor retrieve in readable form. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

choices.text: The pencil referral fails, because a paper document must be written in ink.
The emailed referral succeeds, because electronic transmission is permitted.
Both fail, because a referral must carry a handwritten signature to be valid.
The referral in indelible pencil satisfies the writing requirement.
The emailed referral fails the readable and retrievable requirement.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts collaborating pharmacist learns informally that her supervising physician surrendered his federal controlled substances registration last month. His medical licence is unrestricted and she has received no notice from any board. May she continue co-managing patients this afternoon?

choices.text: No, because the physician is deemed ineligible on that surrender alone.
Yes, because his medical licence remains unrestricted.
Yes, because no board has notified her that anything has changed.
Yes, because only a state registration event affects the collaboration.
Yes, provided she confines herself to non-controlled therapies today.
